a2Note: Yamaha sells an official factory-restricted R7 35kW version in Europe (35.0 kW / 47.6 PS @ 4,500 rpm) for A2 licence holders; the full-power 54 kW bike itself is not A2-compliant.
beginnerNote: The CP2 twin is forgiving and the 35 kW A2 version makes it legally accessible, but committed clip-on ergonomics and supersport geometry are tiring around town — better as a second bike or for a very sport-focused novice.
whoFor: Riders who want genuine R-Series supersport feel and track-day ability without litre-bike power, insurance or intimidation.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you commute daily or carry a passenger — the riding position and tiny pillion pad are uncompromising.
about: The R7 wraps Yamaha's 689cc CP2 parallel twin in a slim full-fairing supersport chassis, updated for 2026 with next-generation R-Series styling and R1-derived technology. At 189 kg wet with 73 PS it prioritises corner speed and rider involvement over outright power. It is one of the few faired supersports still offered with an official 35 kW A2 version in Europe.
pros: Real supersport chassis and looks at middleweight cost
Torquey, easy-going CP2 twin
Light (189 kg wet) and slim, great on twisty roads and track days
Official 35 kW A2 version available
Frugal: 4.1 l/100 km published
cons: Aggressive clip-on riding position tires you in town
Practically no passenger or luggage capability
73 PS is modest next to 4-cylinder rivals

a2Note: Yamaha sells an official factory-restricted MT-07 35kW version in Europe for A2 licence holders; the full-power 54 kW bike itself exceeds A2 limits.
beginnerNote: Light, slim, low-seated and famously easy to ride — one of the default first big bikes in Europe, though the punchy low-end torque and soft-ish suspension reward a little restraint early on.
whoFor: New and returning riders who want one friendly, affordable naked that does town, commute and Sunday twisties with real character.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you ride long motorway distances — there is no wind protection and no cruise control.
about: This is the standard manual-gearbox version of Yamaha's best-selling middleweight naked (the Y-AMT automated version is a separate model). Fully redesigned for 2025, it gained new MT-family styling, a 41 mm USD fork, a 5-inch TFT with smartphone navigation and revised ergonomics while keeping the 689cc CP2 crossplane twin. At 183 kg wet with 68 Nm it remains the benchmark easy-fun middleweight.
pros: Punchy, characterful CP2 twin with strong midrange
Light and slim, 805 mm seat suits most riders
2025 update added USD fork, 5-inch TFT and Garmin StreetCross navigation
Official 35 kW A2 version available
Excellent value and cheap to run (4.1 l/100 km)
cons: No wind protection for motorway work
No cruise control even as an option
Rider aids are basic next to some rivals
sources: Yamaha Motor Europe specifications for the 2025 MT-07 (yamaha-motor.eu product page and product data API)

a2Note: Yamaha does not list an official 35 kW version of the current Ténéré 700 in Europe (spec sheet states limited power version: N/A).
beginnerNote: The engine is friendly and the electronics simple, but an 875 mm seat and 208 kg wet make it a physically demanding first bike, especially off-road or for shorter riders (a factory Low version with 860 mm seat exists).
whoFor: Riders who genuinely take their adventure bike onto gravel and trails and want a mechanically simple, rally-style twin that can still tour.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you are short-legged, mostly ride tarmac, or want radar/IMU-era electronics.
about: The Ténéré 700 pairs the 689cc CP2 twin with a genuine rally-bred chassis: 21/18-inch spoked wheels, long-travel suspension and 240 mm ground clearance. The current generation (2025 redesign, carried into 2026) added ride-by-wire with two throttle maps, a 6.3-inch vertical TFT with MyRide turn-by-turn navigation, switchable ABS and USB-C. It stays deliberately simple and mechanical where rivals pile on electronics.
pros: Real off-road ability: 21/18-inch wheels, 210/200 mm travel, 240 mm clearance
Proven, low-stress CP2 engine with easy torque
16-litre tank and 4.3 l/100 km give ~350 km range
6.3-inch TFT with turn-by-turn navigation and switchable ABS
Strong value against bigger adventure bikes
cons: Tall 875 mm seat and 208 kg wet intimidate shorter riders
Modest 73 PS for fully-loaded two-up motorway touring
No cruise control or IMU-based rider aids
sources: Yamaha Motor Europe specifications for the 2026 Ténéré 700 (yamaha-motor.eu product page and product data API)

a2Note: Yamaha sells an official factory-restricted XSR700 35kW version in several European markets for A2 licence holders; the full-power 54 kW bike itself exceeds A2 limits.
beginnerNote: Mechanically an MT-07 in vintage clothes: light, friendly and torquey with a natural upright riding position, though the 835 mm seat is a touch taller than the MT-07's.
whoFor: Riders who want MT-07 ease and running costs wrapped in 1970s-flavoured styling they can customise.
notFor: Maybe not for you if you want modern-naked tech — the XSR700 keeps a round LED headlight and simple electronics, with no TFT dash or ride modes.
about: The XSR700 is Yamaha's Sport Heritage take on the CP2 platform: the same 689cc crossplane twin and lightweight chassis as the previous-generation MT-07, dressed with a round LED headlight, sculpted metal tank covers and a flat two-tone seat. It rides light and playful at 188 kg wet, and its simplicity is the point — analogue character with modern reliability.
pros: Characterful CP2 twin with easy, flexible torque
Timeless retro styling with quality metal detailing
Light and agile, confidence-inspiring handling
Official 35 kW A2 version available
Popular base for tasteful customisation
cons: Minimal wind protection and small tank limit touring
Basic LCD instruments and no rider modes
Still based on the pre-2025 MT-07 platform
sources: Yamaha Motor Europe specifications for the current XSR700 (yamaha-motor.eu product page and product data API, 2024 model year listing)
